name: Colin Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the folder-gluer at Whitlock and Sons, we make cardboard boxes. The big flat sheets come off the corrugator, and my machine prints them, cuts them, folds them and glues the seam, so out the far end you've got a flat box ready to pop open. I set the knives, mix the ink to the customer's colour, keep the glue right. Twenty years this spring. My dad worked at Whitlock's before me, on the old corrugator.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that old Mr Whitlock still walks the floor and knows your name. His son runs it now but it's still a family place. What wears me out is the dust, cardboard dust gets everywhere, and the rush orders before Christmas. Sundays I'm at church and I do the tea urn in the hall after, my wife Ruth says I'm better at that than the boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's go through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. It was a lot of noise from people in cities selling something. Real work still needs real people. I'd say that at work and to the men at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, same as I'd say out loud. I don't use AI and I don't want to. I'd be glad. My boy Josh is always on at me to try it and I've no interest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Do my job, keep the bit we've saved, about two months, and try to get it to three. We'd keep helping Ruth's mum with her shopping, like always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like getting home and the house is just as you left it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why no interest in trying it, even once?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen what screens do to people. Josh's friends can't hold a conversation. I'd rather learn something with my hands. Call me old-fashioned, I don't mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at Whitlock's that worries you anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big boys, the national box companies, keep undercutting us. That's competition, fair enough, it keeps you honest. But I'd hate to see Whitlock's bought out. Then it's just another plant.

S0.say: I told you so: it was a lot of noise from people in cities selling something. Real work still needs real people, and I'd say that at work and to the men at church.
S0.think: Same as I'd say out loud. I don't use AI and I don't want to, so I'd just be glad.
S0.do: Carries on at Whitlock's and tries to grow two months of savings to three. Keeps helping his wife Ruth's mum with her shopping as usual.
S0.feel: Calm, like coming home to a house just as he left it.
S0.quote: Josh's friends can't hold a conversation. I'd rather learn something with my hands.
S0.fieldNote: Colin's public and private views match closely: he simply doesn't want AI in his life. His bigger worry is a national firm buying out the family business, which he accepts as fair competition. Faith, family and the Whitlock name anchor how he talks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the Whitlocks have always looked after their people and I'd trust them to again. If changes come, they'll come with apprenticeships and training on the job, not a redundancy letter. That's what I'd say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm less sure. Young Mr Whitlock isn't his dad. He went to business school and he talks about efficiency. If the national firms put in robots and cut prices, he'll have to follow or close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down, do good work, and save. No new car, the old estate does fine. Get to four months if I can. I wouldn't go off and learn computers. If Whitlock's wanted me trained on a new machine, I'd do it there, on the job, like I learned this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like hearing a noise from the machine you can't place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd train on the job but not learn computers. Aren't the new machines mostly computers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what they say. But somebody has to set the knives and mix the ink. Maybe. I don't know, honestly. I'd find out when it came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if jobs went at Whitlock's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the Whitlocks. The tech companies, and the government for letting a handful of billionaires decide how the rest of us live. A family firm doesn't stand a chance against that.

S1.say: The Whitlocks have always looked after their people and I'd trust them to again. Change would come with apprenticeships and training on the job, not a redundancy letter.
S1.think: I'm less sure than I let on, because young Mr Whitlock isn't his dad and he talks about efficiency. If the national firms put in robots and cut prices, he'll have to follow or close.
S1.do: Keeps his head down, skips a new car and saves towards four months. Refuses to learn computers on his own but would train on a new machine at work if asked.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like an unfamiliar noise from the machine.
S1.quote: That's what they say. But somebody has to set the knives and mix the ink. Maybe. I don't know, honestly.
S1.fieldNote: Colin's public trust in the Whitlocks covers a real private doubt about the son. He admits he doesn't know whether his hands-on skills survive, which is honest. He blames tech billionaires and a government that lets them, never the family firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong and somebody should stop it. Nobody asked working families. I'd say a family firm can't fight that and the government should protect businesses like Whitlock's, not the tech giants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be frightened. Boxes are simple, a robot could do my whole machine and the one next to it. Two years, Josh would just be starting his last years of school. We'd have two months saved and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut everything. No holiday, cancel the phone upgrades, Ruth would take more hours at the bakery if she could get them. I'd talk to the pastor and the men at church, see who's hiring and who needs a hand. I'd lean on my brother Pete, he's got a building firm, and I'd go labouring for him if I had to. I don't want benefits, but I'd take them before I'd see the kids go short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like the floor's moving and you can't see why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does two years give you time to do anything about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Two years goes in a blink at my age. I'd be praying a lot more than planning, if I'm honest. That's not nothing to me, but it doesn't pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go labouring for Pete. Wouldn't robots reach building work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But Pete's a stubborn man, he'd keep me on out of family. That's how it should work. Family looks after family when the big world doesn't.

S2.say: This is wrong and somebody should stop it, because nobody asked working families. The government should protect businesses like Whitlock's, not the tech giants.
S2.think: I'd be frightened, because boxes are simple and a robot could do my whole machine and the next one. In two years Josh would be in his last years of school and we'd have two months saved and a mortgage.
S2.do: Cuts holidays and phone upgrades while Ruth seeks more bakery hours. Asks the pastor and church men about work, labours for his brother Pete's building firm if needed, and takes benefits only to keep the kids from going short.
S2.feel: Frightened, like the floor moving for no reason he can see.
S2.quote: I'd be praying a lot more than planning, if I'm honest. That's not nothing to me, but it doesn't pay the mortgage.
S2.fieldNote: Colin falls back on faith, church and family rather than retraining or politics. He's candid that prayer won't pay the mortgage. He would accept benefits only as a last resort, which fits his strong dislike of handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to make sure young people get proper apprenticeships, trades that last, before it lands. That's what the government should be spending on. I'd say that at work and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still be on my machine till they turned it off. I'm not going to become a computer man at forty-five. But five years means I could get Josh set up right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get Josh onto an apprenticeship, electrician or plumber, something where you go into people's homes. I'd save hard, overpay a bit on the mortgage, sell the caravan we hardly use. Keep working at Whitlock's as long as there's a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more for the kids than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't robots reach electricians and plumbers too by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in the end. But I'd rather Josh learned a real trade with his hands than sat at a screen. Whatever comes, a man who can fix things is worth something to his neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ruth say about selling the caravan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be sad, it was her dad's. But she's practical, more than me. She'd say it's just a caravan and the kids are the kids.

S3.say: There's time to make sure young people get proper apprenticeships in trades that last before it lands. That's what the government should be spending on.
S3.think: I'd still be on my machine till they turned it off, because I'm not becoming a computer man at forty-five. But five years means I could get Josh set up right.
S3.do: Steers Josh into an electrician or plumbing apprenticeship and sells the little-used caravan that was Ruth's dad's. Saves hard, overpays the mortgage a bit, and stays at Whitlock's as long as the job lasts.
S3.feel: Anxious, more for the kids than for himself.
S3.quote: Whatever comes, a man who can fix things is worth something to his neighbours.
S3.fieldNote: Five years shifts Colin's focus almost entirely to his son's future. He still won't retrain himself, and says so plainly. Selling the caravan of Ruth's late father is a real sacrifice he names without fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time for families and churches and local firms to look after their own, without waiting for the government. That's how it used to work in this town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years I can take. I'd be fifty-three. Josh would be in a trade, Hannah through school, the mortgage nearly paid. I'd probably lose the job in the end, but I'd have done right by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep saving, pay the mortgage down. Get Josh through his apprenticeship and help Hannah with whatever she wants to study. I'd ask Pete about joining his firm at some point, but not yet. Ten years is a long time to change your mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's peace in it. I can do my part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family and church instead of government. What could the church actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plenty. Our church already runs a food bank and a jobs board in the hall. If men are out of work, they can help each other, fix each other's cars, mind kids. It's not a wage, but it's not nothing either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if you lost the job at fifty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to Pete, or anyone who needs a pair of hands. I've never been above any work. My dad swept the floor at Whitlock's for his last two years and held his head up.

S4.say: Ten years is time for families, churches and local firms to look after their own without waiting for the government. That's how it used to work in this town.
S4.think: Ten years I can take: Josh in a trade, Hannah through school, the mortgage nearly paid. I'd probably lose the job in the end, but I'd have done right by them.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving while paying the mortgage down. Sees Josh through his apprenticeship, supports Hannah's studies, and may join his brother Pete's building firm later.
S4.feel: Uneasy but at peace, because he can do his part.
S4.quote: My dad swept the floor at Whitlock's for his last two years and held his head up.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years gives Colin peace because it fits his family timeline. He believes the church can carry people through, pointing to its food bank and jobs board. His pride in honest work of any kind comes straight from his father.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time to get the kids set up and no time to save. What would help is the government backing family firms and apprenticeships instead of letting the big tech companies run everything, and a bit of breathing room on the mortgage if you lose your job through no fault of your own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You might ask about pride. A man who's worked since sixteen doesn't want a cheque for sitting at home. Give me any job, even a lesser one, before you give me money for nothing.

headlineQuote: A man who's worked since sixteen doesn't want a cheque for sitting at home.
portrait: Colin Moreau, 43, has run the folder-gluer at Whitlock and Sons, a family-owned cardboard box maker, for twenty years, following his father into the firm. He never uses AI, is wary of screens, and leans on faith, church and family. He publicly trusts the Whitlocks to look after their people but privately doubts the owner's son. AGI in two years frightens him because there's no time to save or set up his children, while with more time his focus turns almost entirely to getting his son Josh into a trade and paying down the mortgage, never to retraining himself.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because there would be no time to save or to get his children set up.
whatWouldHelp: Government backing for family firms and apprenticeships rather than big tech, and breathing room on the mortgage for people who lose their jobs through no fault of their own.
